newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's new cosmodrome runs into maiden launch row.
newsitem.headline: Russia's new cosmodrome runs into maiden launch row.

text.p: Russia opened its new cosmodrome in the Far East on Tuesday with the launch of a military satellite -- and ran straight into a row with the ethnic region of Yakutia.
Yakutia is where jettisoned parts of booster rockets from the launchpad fall to Earth and the diamond-rich republic is angry it was not told about Tuesday's firing.

Yegor Borisov, deputy head of Yakutia's government, told Interfax news agency he was filing a claim against the head of Russia's military space forces because the launch had not been authorised by Yakutia.
Interfax said the authorities would also recommend to the local parliament the scrapping of a treaty between Moscow and Yakutia, which allows for jettisoning over the thinly populated region.

The Start-1 booster rocket and its secret military satellite blasted off at 0200 GMT from the cosmodrome, which is still being built at a snowbound former strategic nuclear missile base in Siberia about 9,000 km (6,000 miles) east of Moscow and just 100 km (60 miles) from the Chinese border.
Itar-Tass news agency said the second stage of the booster rocket fell "with a deafening thunder" in Yaktuia near the tiny village of Keptin early on Tuesday, six minutes after the launch.
Yakutia officials, saying they doubted the safety of the Start rocket, had warned the Defence Ministry in a letter before the launch that they may scrap the 1996 agreement with Moscow.
On Monday protesters, apparently with the backing of the local authorities, reportedly took to the streets of Yakutsk, capital of the ethnic republic of Sakha-Yakutia, north of the new cosmodrome.
"One cannot trample over the demands of the people to boost the military-space complex budget," Borisov said.
Svobodny is destined to be the main launch pad for the commercial satellites Moscow is banking on to fund its financially troubled space industry.
The new cosmodrome was developed on orders from President Boris Yeltsin to to reduce dependence on the main Soviet launch site at Baikonur, which Moscow now has to rent from independent Kazakhstan.
Deputy head of the military space forces General Vyacheslav Artyomenko told Itar-Tass he thought the launch had been premature.
"It (the decision to launch) was an astonishing surprise. We have to respect the people living next to us, the people we serve," he said.
